extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students, researchers and professionals seeking an overview of peer review
extracted.subtask_description: A broad encyclopedic summary of peer review: definitions, purposes, types (scholarly, medical, technical, pedagogical), common practices (anonymity, decision outcomes), criticisms, and suggested improvements/alternatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peer review definition and purposes
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer review is the evaluation of work by one or more people with similar competencies as the producers of the work (peers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It functions as a form of self-regulation by qualified members of a profession within the relevant field. Peer review methods are used to maintain quality standards, improve performance, and provide credibility. In academia, scholarly peer review is typically used to determine an academic paper's suitability for publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer qualifications and anonymity
rubrics_metrics.description: The reviewers are experts in the topic at hand and they have no connection to the author (they are not told the name of the author). They are anonymous and cannot be pressured.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anonymity (single-, double-, or other blinding) is a key mechanism intended to reduce conflicts of interest and pressure on reviewers; top journals use such practices and may reject a high percentage of submissions (>90%).

rubrics_metrics.name: Scholarly peer review decision categories
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer review is used to inform decisions related to whether the work should be accepted, considered acceptable with revisions, or rejected for official publication in an academic journal, monograph, or conference proceedings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editorial processes (editor-in-chief, editorial board, program committee) use reviewers' reports to make these determinations; dual-anonymous review is one variant where identities of authors are not revealed to reviewers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement for a qualified, impartial community of experts
rubrics_metrics.description: Academic peer review requires a community of experts in a given (and often narrowly defined) academic field, who are qualified and able to perform reasonably impartial review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Impartiality can be difficult—especially in interdisciplinary fields—because significance may not be widely appreciated by contemporaries. The page notes that impartial review is a substantive criterion but can be hard to achieve in practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Medical peer review classifications
rubrics_metrics.description: Medical peer review may be distinguished in four classifications: clinical peer review; peer evaluation of clinical teaching skills; scientific peer review of journal articles; a secondary round of peer review for clinical value of concurrently published articles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The term 'medical peer review' is used variably (including by AMA) to mean both improving quality/safety in health care organizations and rating clinical behavior or membership compliance; terminology and standardization are imperfect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clinical peer review (healthcare quality & credentialing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Clinical peer review is a procedure for assessing a patient's involvement with experiences of care and is an element of ongoing professional practice assessment—important for provider credentialing and privileging.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used within healthcare institutions to evaluate clinical performance, document teaching scholarship, and support privileging/credentialing decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical peer review (engineering)
rubrics_metrics.description: Technical peer reviews are a well-defined review process for finding and fixing defects, conducted by a team of peers with assigned roles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typically carried out by peers representing areas of the life cycle affected by the material being reviewed (usually limited to 6 or fewer people). Technical peer reviews are held within development phases, between milestone reviews, on completed products or completed portions of products.

rubrics_metrics.name: Professional peer review purpose (performance/certification)
rubrics_metrics.description: Professional peer review focuses on the performance of professionals, with a view to improving quality, upholding standards, or providing certification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include historical physician-review practices where local councils examined practitioners' notes to judge whether care met required standards; many fields (accounting, law, engineering, aviation) employ such processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pedagogical peer review (student peer assessment)
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer review (student peer assessment) is a collaborative learning tool used in secondary and post-secondary education as part of the writing process, where groups of students review each other's work and provide feedback and suggestions for revision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is used to build connection, develop writer identity, and help students understand how different readers perceive their work; forms may closely mimic scholarly peer review or use adapted classroom variants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classroom peer review best practices and instructor scaffolding
rubrics_metrics.description: Instructors may provide examples, model peer review with the class, or focus on specific areas of feedback during the peer review process. They may experiment with in-class peer review vs. peer review as homework, or use learning-management-system technologies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Other recommended practices: segment the peer review process into groups, have students present papers while others take notes, expand review scope to the entire class, ask reviewers to answer three focused questions about a paper, and consider using instructional assistants to provide more expert feedback.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peer seminar format and expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer seminar involves a speaker presenting ideas to an audience that also acts as a 'contest'—multiple speakers present in turn with time limits and may be interrupted by audience questions and feedback.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This format allows more personal presentation and interactive critique; it is similar to conference talks but typically allows more time and direct audience interruption for feedback.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critiques, biases, and common pitfalls of peer review
rubrics_metrics.description: Criticisms include role duality (being both evaluator and evaluated), bias against 'negative studies', systemic subjectivity, lack of standardization, and that peer review does not prevent publication of invalid research.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In classroom contexts: lack of training, limited engagement, time constraints, emotional factors, and superficial feedback can all undermine effectiveness. Editorial gatekeeping and unverifiable rejections are also cited as systemic problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence on effectiveness and limits of peer review
rubrics_metrics.description: Direct evidence that peer review improves quality of published papers is scarce; peer review does not prevent publication of invalid research, though some controlled analyses have found substantive improvements between submission and publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article cites randomized-trial analyses showing editorial and peer review processes can lead to substantive improvement; however, experimentally controlled studies are hard to arrange, and the overall evidence base is limited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alternatives and comparisons (including self-assessment and lotteries)
rubrics_metrics.description: Various alternatives to peer review have been suggested (such as funding-by-lottery). Some studies show self-assessment can produce significant improvement compared to peer review in certain classroom experiments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comparisons suggest self-checking may better clarify revision goals; educators have recommended other models (instructional assistants, segmented review, online tools) to address weaknesses of peer review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of technology and AI in peer review
rubrics_metrics.description: New tools could help alter the peer review process: online peer review software can provide editing tools, guided question lists, and allow multiple comment types; artificial intelligence has been reported to assist or perform peer review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Benefits include structured guidance for reviewers and traceable comments; risks include undisclosed AI use and attempts to manipulate automated processes (e.g., preprint prompting to influence automated refereeing).

rubrics_metrics.name: Government and policy peer review procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: In policy contexts (EU example), a 'host country' lays a given policy open to examination by other countries and relevant NGOs; meetings are preceded by an expert report, peer countries submit comments, meetings include visits to local sites, and results are published.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some jurisdictions mandate scientific peer review (e.g., California requires independent external scientific peer review of scientific findings underpinning rulemaking). Peer review in policy often emphasizes transparency, expert reports, site visits, and publication of results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Review structure, assigned roles, and process timing
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer review involves structured roles (editor-in-chief, editorial board, program committee, reviewers) and—especially in technical reviews—assigned reviewer roles; timing can include in-development-phase reviews, between milestone reviews, or on completed portions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicit role assignment and timing (e.g., limited team size for technical reviews) are recommended practices to make reviews effective at finding and fixing defects and to align reviews with development lifecycles.
